en: Udāna 8.8 Visākhāsutta Thus have I heard:
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in the Eastern Park, in the Mansion of Migāra’s Mother.
Now at that time Visākhā, the daughter of Migāra’s mother, had died—she who was dear and beloved.

Then Visākhā, the daughter of Migāra’s mother, with wet clothes and wet hair, went to the Blessed One during the middle of the day; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, she sat down to one side.
As Visākhā, Migāra’s mother, was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to her:
“Well now, Visākhā, where have you come from, with your clothes wet and your hair wet, arriving here in the middle of the day?
“Venerable sir, my dear and beloved granddaughter has passed away.”
"Therefore, with my clothes wet and my hair wet, I have come here during the day.
"Visākhā, would you wish to have as many sons and grandsons as there are people in Sāvatthī?
"I would wish, Blessed One, to have as many sons and grandsons as there are people in Sāvatthī."
“But how many people, Visākhā, die every day in Sāvatthī?
“Ten people, Bhante, die every day in Sāvatthī;
nine people, Bhante….”
Even eight, venerable sir… even seven,
venerable sir… even six, venerable sir…
Even five, venerable sir… even four,
venerable sir… even three, venerable sir…
"Venerable sir, two people die every day in Sāvatthī;
even one person dies every day in Sāvatthī.
Venerable sir, Sāvatthī is never devoid of people who are dying."
“What do you think, Visākhā, have you ever at any time been without washed clothes or without washed hair?
“Certainly not, Bhante.
Enough for me, Bhante, with so many sons and grandsons.”
“Indeed, Visākhā, for those who have a hundred loves, there are a hundred sufferings;
for those who have ninety loves, there are ninety sufferings;
for those who have eighty loves, there are eighty sufferings.”
For those who have seventy loves, there are seventy sufferings;
for those who have sixty loves, there are sixty sufferings;
for those who have fifty loves, there are fifty sufferings.
For those who have forty dear things, there are forty sufferings;
for those who have thirty dear things, there are thirty sufferings;
for those who have twenty dear things, there are twenty sufferings.
For those who have ten dear things, they have ten sufferings;
for those who have nine dear things, they have nine sufferings;
for those who have eight dear things, they have eight sufferings.
For those who have seven dear things, they have seven sufferings;
for those who have six dear things, they have six sufferings;
for those who have five dear things, they have five sufferings.
For those who have four dear things, they have four sufferings;
for those who have three dear things, they have three sufferings;
for those who have two dear things, they have two sufferings.
“For those who have one thing dear, there is suffering for them;
for those who have nothing dear, there is no suffering for them. They are sorrowless, stainless, and free from despair—so I say.
Then the Blessed One, having understood this matter, on that occasion uttered this inspired exclamation (udāna):
“Whatever sorrows or lamentations there are,
whatever various kinds of suffering exist in the world—
all these arise dependent upon what is dear.”
When there is no endearment, these do not exist.
Therefore, those for whom there is nothing anywhere in the world that is dear are happy and free from sorrow.
Therefore, one who desires sorrowlessness and freedom from passion should not form attachment to anything whatsoever in the world.
Thus ends the eighth [verse].
